<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Air pollution is a significant environmental issue with widespread impacts on public health. Evidence on the causal effect of air pollution control policies on weight‐related outcomes remains limited. This study fills this gap by leveraging the Air Pollution Prevention and Control Action Plan as a quasi‐natural experiment, combining four waves (2010, 2012, 2014, 2016) of panel data from the China Family Panel Studies (CFPS). Employing a difference‐in‐differences framework, we find that implementing this policy significantly reduces overweight risk among residents. Mechanism analyses indicate that the policy primarily lowers overweight risk by increasing physical exercise frequency and alleviating depressive symptoms. Further heterogeneity analyses show this impact is particularly pronounced among urban residents, young adults, females, and individuals with lower educational attainment. Our findings clarify the causal link between environmental regulation and population health, and provide actionable insights for policymakers to design coordinated interventions that leverage air quality improvements to advance public health goals.</jats:p>

title: Production Function Estimation for China: A State Space Time Series Analysis considering Quality of Labor Forces

10.1017/s0022109025102123.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Using model-free skewness measures that exploit the asymmetry in semivariances and option data from the over-the-counter currency market, we find that buying currencies with a high skewness risk premium (SRP) and selling currencies with a low SRP generates high returns and a Sharpe ratio. Asset pricing tests—which control for omitted variables and measurement errors—show that a SRP factor enters the currency pricing kernel and is central to the pricing of risks inherent in a broad currency cross section of 60 portfolio excess returns. These results imply that skewness risk is a strong and priced source of currency risk.</jats:p>

                  <jats:p>This study investigates the potential benefits of intellectual property rights (IPR) institutions for international production networks. Using unique data on manufacturer-supplier linkages in the automotive industry, we establish a positive empirical relationship between the efficiency of vehicle producers and IPR protection in their suppliers’ locations. Notably, IPR do not have the same impact on ownership networks as knowledge is internalized within the boundaries of the firm. We confirm that the results are not driven by other firm- or country-level characteristics, and address potential endogeneity concerns by employing a novel gravity-based IV approach using geographical distance and language proximity.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Sustainability standards are central to the governance of global value chains, shaping labour conditions and environmental practices. Yet established scholarship privileges standards originating in the Global North, creating a significant gap in understanding how sustainability governance is shaped for and within the Global South. Through a comparative analysis of standards in South African wine and Indian tea, this article shows that Southern standards are produced through relational and trans-scalar struggles embedded in uneven material power relations within and across value chains. By tracing their interaction with established Northern regimes, the article reconceptualises sustainability governance as a contested and polycentric field.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This paper explores the role of Standard Essential Patents (SEPs) in shaping technological development and regional innovation in Europe’s telecommunications sector. Results reveal strong geographic concentration: Helsinki and Stockholm account for one-third of all cellular SEPs. Unlike other technologies, SEP distribution does not scale with population or prior technological expertise. Findings suggest a “rich-get-richer” dynamic where early leadership reinforces future dominance; however, this advantage weakens across technological generations. This study offers new insights into standardization’s spatial dynamics and underscores the need for long-term perspectives when modeling technological competition and diffusion.</jats:p>

10.1093/jeg/lbag046.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Rising geopolitical tensions and emerging skepticism against globalization cast doubt on the future evolution of European regional economic growth. We simulate regional GDP growth rates for all NUTS2 regions in the EU27+UK for the period 2021–2035, using the MASST5 model, in two extreme scenarios; the first, termed “Cohesive EU in an Integrated World”; the second, labeled “Nationalistic EU in a Fragmented World”. Results document substantial spatial heterogeneity in the outcomes of the two scenarios, with Integration leading to superior economic performance but at the cost of increasing regional disparities triggered by higher growth opportunities for national champions.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>As the Journal of Economic Geography turns 25, this commentary reflects on the field’s representations of care and directions for future research. In much of economic geography, care remains an absence, deemed peripheral to the economy. Yet for decades, scholars have shown that care exerts a pervasive influence as a foundation of economic activity. Care is also an increasingly important frontier for firms, finance and technology. Finally, care acts as a catalyst for rethinking and reorganising economic geographies. Reviewing existing work, I outline research agendas to address the distorting marginalisation of care and its transformative potential.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>We analyze how the proliferation of short-term rentals (STRs) affects firm survival, performance, and entry in two European cities with high STR density. Using administrative firm-level accounting data, a shift-share instrument, and an event-study design, we find that STR growth increases exit rates among underperforming firms, while surviving firms experience relative gains in sales and profits, with no effects on employment or investment. Corporate tax revenues accruing to the central government also rise, pointing to broader fiscal spillovers. STR expansion stimulates entrepreneurship, though new entrants face higher costs and lower initial profitability. These findings underscore the nuanced impacts of tourism-driven demand shocks on urban economic ecosystems.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This paper analyzes the political processes by which time zones are locally managed and changed, and how these are converted into global standards in the absence of an international time zone standardization body. We argue that the persistence of a singular global time zone standard depends on technical infrastructures operating largely independently of state and non-state actors. The apparent neutrality of time zones as technical artifacts supporting international coordination required for economic globalization obscures locally negotiated practices shaped by social, biological, political, and economic rationales. The study highlights how globally uniform technical systems can coexist with locally differentiated yet politically contested practices.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This study examines the role that the location of transaction partners plays in firms’ location choice. To alleviate endogeneity concerns, we use data of Japanese firms that were forced to relocate due to the massive Tohoku earthquake in 2011. We find that firms tended to relocate to cities where their customers were located rather than where their suppliers were located. Firms also tended to relocate to cities where their banks were located. The positive role that the presence of customers and banks played in firms’ relocation choice was weaker if their customers and banks were also damaged by the earthquake.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The relationship between industrial districts and firm sustainability orientation has gained attention; however, systematic evidence remains limited. This study investigates how value chain positioning, distinguishing business-to-business firms from business-to-consumer firms, interacts with industrial district locations in shaping environmental sustainability orientation. Using data on 1083 Italian fashion firms, we combined financial information from ORBIS and AIDA with web-scraped sustainability indicators. OLS and instrumental variable estimations show that firms located in industrial districts exhibit a stronger environmental sustainability orientation, with effects particularly pronounced among B2B firms operating within districts. These findings offer important implications for entrepreneurs, sustainability managers, policymakers, and stakeholders.</jats:p>

10.1093/jeg/lbag053.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>While the literature on the Internet’s economic impact often focuses on skill-biased technological change, less is known about its effect on employer market power. This article asks whether the arrival of high-speed Internet can weaken firms’ monopsony power, particularly in a developing country context. Using firm-level data from China and leveraging the quasi-exogenous expansion of broadband Internet around the year 2000 in a difference-in-differences design, we find that broadband access leads to a significant reduction in firm-level wage markdowns. This effect is driven by four channels: reduced search frictions, increased labor mobility, enhanced firm entry, and stronger worker bargaining power. The resulting decline in labor market power is associated with a higher labor share of income and an increased pass-through of productivity gains to wages. Our findings challenge the conventional view that information and communications technology exacerbates inequality, demonstrating that by promoting labor market competition, it can also have a significant pro-labor equalizing effect.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This article studies the local economic and innovation spillovers from subsidiaries of domestically large firms in China. I construct a geo-referenced dataset linking subsidiaries of publicly listed firms (PLFSs) to the universe of patent applications and nighttime lights (NTL), and iteratively select newly established PLFSs in areas without pre-existing nearby listed-firm subsidiaries. Using a staggered difference-in-differences design that compares earlier- and later-entry locations, I estimate the local effect of a single PLFS at a granular spatial scale. PLFS entry increases local economic activity and innovation, raising NTL by 26.4 per cent and local patenting by 95 per cent within 2.5 km. Firm-level decomposition shows both incumbent innovation gains and more innovative entry, suggesting localized innovation growth rather than pure relocation. Further inventor-level analysis provides evidence of creative destruction, as local innovation paths shift, with pre-existing inventors being replaced by new ones. These findings highlight the role of mega-firm subsidiaries in driving local economies and inform the design of firm-specific place-based policies.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This article reviews how evolving institutions shaped China’s economic geography since the reform era. The review covers three areas. First, we examine reductions in spatial frictions through hukou reform and transportation expansion, and their effects on migration, productivity, welfare, and spatial inequality. Second, we review urban and rural land reforms, housing reform, land-based public finance, and the promotion tournament, which improved allocation but distorted land use, infrastructure, and local debt. Third, we discuss place-based policies and agglomeration, including special economic zones as bundled institutions combining economic incentives with political support. We highlight China’s contribution to core questions in economic geography.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This article examines how transport mode shapes the geography of exchange rate pass-through (ERPT) within Global Value Chains. Using transaction-level customs data from the Bangladeshi garment sector (2018–24), we exploit the sharp depreciation of the Bangladeshi Taka in 2022 to compare maritime and air-based trade corridors through Chittagong seaport and Dhaka airport. We show that ERPT to exporter prices is incomplete on average and systematically lower in buyer–seller relationships that rely more intensively on air transport. This differential is concentrated in destinations and products where delivery speed is especially valuable, notably European fast-fashion markets.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This study investigates the role of domestic production networks in transmitting lockdown shocks originating in upstream and downstream provinces and shaping export performance in the focal province. Using a firm-to-firm transaction-based interprovincial input–output table to construct exposure measures, we find that a one-standard-deviation increase in downstream lockdown exposure reduces export growth by 13.6 log points, whereas upstream lockdown exposure has negligible effects. The impact is short-lived and concentrated in ordinary trade, differentiated products, and durable goods. These findings indicate complementarity between domestic sales and exports. Our evidence supports the economies of scale channel over liquidity constraints.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This study explores the potential of transport networks in promoting inter-jurisdictional market integration. Utilizing over 3 million public procurement contracts, we assess the impact of China’s recent high-speed rail (HSR) expansion on the flow of government contracts across cities. HSR connections significantly increased cross-city procurement within provinces but had negligible impact on cross-province dyads. With data on both accepted and rejected bidders, we find that while out-of-province firms increased bid participation, their winning probabilities decreased after HSR connections. Our results suggest that administrative borders undermine the positive impact of transportation infrastructure on domestic market integration.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This article estimates the effect of gender quotas in local politics on female entrepreneurship. We exploit the introduction of a 2012 Italian reform mandating female candidate representation in municipal elections for municipalities above 5,000 inhabitants, and implement a difference-in-differences event-study design comparing municipalities first exposed to the reform with never-treated municipalities, restricting attention to a narrow population window around the binding threshold. Using a balanced panel of 607 municipalities observed from 2007 to 2022, we find that quota exposure increases female entrepreneurship by approximately 2–3 per cent. The effect is concentrated in regions with lower baseline gender equality, consistent with a catch-up mechanism whereby female political visibility matters most where it is most novel. We find no evidence that the effect operates through increased municipal spending on childcare or social-care services, providing no support for the most natural policy channels. The evidence is instead broadly consistent with a role-model interpretation: the increased visibility of women in local political leadership appears to shift the perceived feasibility of entrepreneurial entry among women in gender-unequal environments.</jats:p>

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>We examine the adoption of expanded audit reports that include key audit matters (KAMs) in Hong Kong (2016) and mainland China (2017). These jurisdictions are highly integrated and together constitute one of the largest economies to adopt the IAASB's reporting standards in a staggered fashion, while also differing in investor protection and legal enforcement. Using matched samples, pre‐post tests, and staggered difference‐in‐differences analyses with company fixed effects, we do not find compelling evidence that expanded audit reports affect market reactions or audit quality. These findings suggest a substantial gap between regulatory intent and implementation—on average, in these markets, KAMs do not appear to meet investors' demand for incremental information or to improve audit quality substantially. At the same time, our cross‐sectional evidence on KAM characteristics is more nuanced. A higher number of KAMs and the presence of novel or transaction‐specific KAMs are associated with stronger pricing of fundamentals, consistent with investors perceiving the related financial statements as better vetted. Yet a higher number of KAMs and novel KAMs are also associated with lower profitability persistence, consistent with these disclosures reflecting company risk and volatility. In contrast, industry‐common KAMs appear less relevant for valuation, consistent with investors discounting routine disclosures, even though they are associated with more persistent performance likely reflecting more stable industry conditions. Overall, our evidence suggests that mandating expanded audit reports alone may be of limited value, whereas better tailored KAM disclosures may still serve as signals of firm fundamentals and future performance.</jats:p>

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Over the past decade, live streaming e‐commerce (LSEC) has become a key driver of agri‐food marketing transformation and rural economic revitalization, yet it lacks systematic synthesis of empirical evidence specific to this domain, leading to fragmented insights and limited practical guidance that hinder sustainable, inclusive agri‐food system development. Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews (PRISMA) framework and SPIDER protocol, this systematic review maps core research topics (consumer outcomes, supply chain optimization, and technology application), theories, methods, and implications based on 68 peer‐reviewed journal articles indexed in Web of Science during 2016–2025. It contributes to agri‐food systems and e‐commerce literature by proposing standardized terminology and unified definitions for key constructs, developing a conceptual framework linking core research topics to multi‐dimensional value enhancement, and advancing a supply chain model delineating key stakeholder interactions in agri‐food LSEC—collectively informing agricultural modernization, rural development, and agri‐food system resilience. The review also highlights critical limitations and offers targeted future research directions, providing comprehensive actionable insights for policymakers, practitioners, and researchers to advance the creation of economic, social, and environmental values through LSEC in the agri‐food sector.</jats:p>

                  <jats:p>
                    This systematic review critically examines empirical research on retirement financial planning (RFP) in China, framed by the PRISMA guidelines and the “C‐RFP‐C” protocol. The protocol is registered at OSF (
                    <jats:ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="https://osf.io/f3nps">https://osf.io/f3nps</jats:ext-link>
                    ). Specialized databases such as EconLit, Business Source Premier, ABI/INFORM, Social Sciences Citation Index, and AgeLine were used, as well as multidisciplinary databases and Chinese‐language sources (CNKI and Wanfang). The search strategies employed yielded a total of 2035 documents related to RFP within the Chinese context. After rigorous screening and quality appraisal, 55 studies met the established inclusion criteria and were synthesized qualitatively. The synthesis highlights the central role of financial literacy in RFP, alongside the influence of psychological, social, and institutional factors. Across studies, persistent disparities emerge across gender and between urban and rural populations. Motivational factors such as future orientation and goal clarity shape willingness to plan and save, while opportunities for retirement planning are strongly conditioned by income, asset ownership, pension design, and access to financial and digital infrastructure. Overall, the findings underscore the multidimensional and context‐dependent nature of RFP in China, as structured by the interaction of capacity, willingness, and opportunity.

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Changing the agrifood system is necessary to achieve the global Sustainable Development Goals and close the gap between urban and rural areas. Conventional monocentric growth models frequently emphasize the urban core to the detriment of rural hinterlands. This article surveys how regional polycentricity and multi‐dimensional connection facilitate the inclusive transformation of rural areas. We offer a thorough synthesis of multidisciplinary research that connects spatial configuration, physical transport connectivity, specifically high‐speed rail, and inclusive digital infrastructure. We emphasize the synergistic mechanisms by which physical and digital connectivity enable smallholders to be incorporated into restructured global value chains and empower underprivileged communities. We critically assess the impact of digitalization in improving green agricultural output and climate resilience, acknowledging the nonlinear dynamics of the adoption of technology across various geographical contexts. This article gathers evidence on sustainable and resilient agrifood systems and proposes a future research agenda focused on smart territorial linkages and the effects of global environmental shocks on systems. These results confirm that an inclusive agrifood revolution requires the careful planning of regional space and investments in physical and digital infrastructure, if social equality and environmental sustainability is to endure.</jats:p>

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The widespread diffusion of artificial intelligence (AI) has delivered a systemic shock to the global labor market, making it a central concern in macroeconomic policy and social governance. This paper systematically reviews 180 representative articles published in leading journals between 2000 and March 2026, with the aim of clarifying the transmission mechanisms and economic consequences of AI‐induced structural changes in employment. Using bibliometric and qualitative analyses, we show that research output in this field is strongly shaped by major technological breakthroughs—especially generative AI—and is geographically concentrated in economies such as the United States and China. We document a shift from static, aggregate measures of technological exposure toward dynamic, multidimensional vulnerability frameworks that integrate task content and micro‐level worker characteristics. We further synthesize evidence that AI's labor‐market impacts arise from interactions among technological attributes, individual endowments, organizational heterogeneity, and institutional environments. The resulting economic effects are asymmetric and mixed: productivity gains coexist with factor‐income polarization, while new skill demands are accompanied by heightened displacement risks, skill mismatches, and occupational insecurity. We conclude by outlining a future research agenda that addresses data limitations, identification challenges, and cross‐country comparability, and that supports dynamic, context‐sensitive policy responses.</jats:p>

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The advancement of global agrifood systems increasingly relies on digital innovation; however, the inclusive potential of digital agricultural productive services (APS) remains a subject of intense debate. This paper offers a systematic literature review (SLR) of some articles published between 2011 and 2026. We develop a unified conceptual framework based on Transaction Cost Economics (TCE) and the Capability Approach to analyze the mechanisms through which digitalization mitigates market frictions and empowers marginalized rural stakeholders, including smallholders, women, and youth. The review shows that digital APS makes it much cheaper for farmers to find and hire workers and improve their noncognitive skills. However, the resulting inclusive outcomes are often not linear and depend on “threshold effects” of infrastructure and institutional development. We also find that there are significant gaps in our knowledge about how digitalization will affect agricultural productivity in the long term, how it might enhance climate resilience, and how it might facilitate trade that is open to everyone. The study concludes with a strategic research agenda, and we recommend particular policies that aim to bridge the “soft” digital divide and establish inclusive data governance frameworks to ensure equitable transformations within the agrifood system.</jats:p>

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Nature and biodiversity loss have recently gained prominence as a critical dimension of environmental risk for the financial sector. Unlike climate change, integrating biodiversity considerations into financial decision‐making is far more intricate and methodologically heterogeneous. This paper presents a systematic literature review (SLR) of 22 peer‐reviewed studies published between 2011 and 2025, synthesizing the current state of knowledge on how financial institutions identify, assess, and manage nature‐related risks. The evidence reveals limited but increasing attention to biodiversity within banks, insurers, and asset managers, predominantly driven by regulatory developments, reputational concerns and internal capabilities. Empirical studies suggest that biodiversity loss can generate both physical and transition risks, with potential systemic implications for financial stability. At the same time, financial intermediaries are gradually developing tools and frameworks to integrate nature‐related risks into disclosure, risk management and investment strategies. This review identifies financial institutions as active players whose capital‐allocation decisions can accelerate the transition toward biodiversity conservation and outlines key priorities for future research.</jats:p>

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Business failure research has expanded rapidly, yet much of the review literature remains focused on cataloguing methods rather than explaining their economic relevance. This article organizes the literature around four analytical dimensions: predictive versus causal orientation, static versus dynamic modelling, interpretability versus accuracy, and the degree of macroeconomic integration. Combining bibliometric mapping with interpretive synthesis, the paper examines how model development reflects changing data environments, decision requirements, and regulatory constraints. The analysis shows a shift from static, interpretable models based on accounting data toward dynamic, data‐rich, and increasingly AI‐driven approaches. However, improved predictive performance does not automatically translate into economic value. Model usefulness depends on temporal robustness, decision relevance, and compatibility with governance requirements. In this context, explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) provides a means to reconcile predictive accuracy with interpretability and regulatory usability. The review contributes by integrating accounting, finance, econometrics, and machine learning into a unified analytical framework and by clarifying when different modelling approaches are economically meaningful. It shows that evaluation must extend beyond classification accuracy to include economic loss, intervention timing, and macro‐financial conditions. The paper concludes with a research agenda emphasizing external validity, multimodal systems, and decision‐oriented evaluation standards.</jats:p>

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This paper provides a comprehensive review of the literature on taxation policy within the framework of strategic market games (SMG). We refer to a simple prototype of SMGs called bilateral oligopoly models. The review reveals that the effects and effectiveness of redistributive tax policies depend on individuals' preferences and strategic behavior in trade. Central to this analysis is the influence of strategic interactions on the price formation mechanism and, therefore, on the optimality of tax and transfer policies for improving allocation efficiency. We connect our findings to broader discussions on tax incidence and optimal taxation in environments characterized by market imperfections, market power, and strategic interactions. Although we consider different fiscal instruments, this review points to a common underlying mechanism: the incidence and optimality of taxation depend on key factors such as preferences and the design of tax instruments. In this sense, this survey highlights the complementarity of a diverse and growing literature.</jats:p>

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This study conducts a systematic review of 149 records, including peer‐reviewed articles, reports, working papers, and theses, to empirically investigate the gender pay gap and the factors that contribute to it in organizations. The study has three primary objectives: (1) To identify and analyze the determinants of the gender wage gap in the workforce, (2) To examine how these determinants differ across high‐income, low‐income, upper‐middle‐income, and lower‐middle‐income countries, and (3) To review and propose tailored policy implications and recommendations. The findings reveal that social barriers, occupational segregation, and unpaid care work are key drivers of the gender wage gap worldwide. While legal, economic, and societal measures have made progress in reducing wage inequality, persistent gaps remain, particularly in non‐OECD and low‐income countries, where data is scarce. To address these disparities, the study emphasizes the need for legal enforcement, wage transparency, and anti‐discrimination regulations. It also highlights the importance of education and family‐friendly policies in supporting women's employment and reducing the motherhood penalty. Valuing unpaid care work and promoting gender diversity are essential for creating a more inclusive labor market. This study offers a global analysis of the gender wage gap, providing insights and highlighting research gaps.</jats:p>

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Innovation adoption in the agro‐food sector is essential for enhancing productivity, sustainability, and maintaining competitiveness in the European Union. Both firms and farms in this sector face a complex landscape of drivers and barriers that influence their ability to adopt new technologies and practices. The paper employs a structured literature review approach to analyze existing studies on this topic. Focusing on separate analyses for farms and firms, our investigation began with a selection of 165 studies. After excluding book chapters, books, and conference papers, and including only those pertinent to member states, we reviewed abstracts to narrow our selection to a total of 56 papers. Several findings have emerged from this analysis. Public funding is a major driver, providing essential financial support, though it can be less accessible for micro and small to medium enterprises. Knowledge spillovers and collaboration along the supply chain are crucial for disseminating innovative practices. The role of the Internet of Things is increasingly significant, offering solutions for supply chain management. Investments in research and development are pivotal for technological advancements. Differences exist between the innovation drivers and barriers for farms and firms, indicating the need for tailored approaches to support innovation across the sector.</jats:p>

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>With the mounting pressure on the global ecological environment, the allocation of financial resources must be premised on promoting the green transformation of the economic system. Issues related to sustainable finance and regional ecological resilience have become research hotspots in current fields such as environmental economics and finance. This paper presents a comprehensive review on the relationship between sustainable finance and regional ecological resilience. By sorting out the core connotations, evolutionary contexts and measurement methods of sustainable finance and regional ecological resilience, and based on environmental finance theory, ecological resilience theory and regional sustainable development theory, it analyzes the interaction mechanisms between sustainable finance and regional ecological resilience as documented in the literature across different national and regional contexts, based on a bibliometric and thematic synthesis of empirical studies. Furthermore, it provides policy references and practical guidance from the perspectives of improving the sustainable financial system and strengthening the regional ecological governance mechanism.</jats:p>

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    This paper provides a bibliometric mapping and economic interpretation of the literature on competition in higher education. Drawing on 1470 Scopus‐indexed articles (1961–2023), we combine descriptive bibliometrics, a keyword co‐occurrence network, and a multiple correspondence analysis (MCA) of harmonized author‐assigned keywords with a unified economic framework that distinguishes two functions of competition: an
                    <jats:italic>evaluative–optimizing</jats:italic>
                    mechanism, in which institutions are compared against criteria treated as known in advance, and a
                    <jats:italic>generative–discovery</jats:italic>
                    mechanism, in which decentralized experimentation reveals information that cannot be fully specified beforehand. Both the co‐occurrence network (modularity ) and the MCA reveal a pronounced conceptual asymmetry: the field is organized around a large, central, internally elaborated vocabulary of rankings, performance, quality assurance, reputation, efficiency, and institutional positioning, while discovery‐oriented concerns—innovation, institutional diversity, scientific incentives, and the organization of knowledge production—are less central and less coherently consolidated within the retained author‐keyword structure. We connect this asymmetry to the policy chronology—massification, performance‐based funding, deregulation, the Bologna process, and global rankings—through which the evaluative–optimizing function has been progressively institutionalized. The contribution is threefold: a large‐scale map of the field, an economic distinction between two functions of competition, and a reading of why the literature's conceptual structure has taken its present, asymmetric form.
                  </jats:p>

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>With time, adaptation finance (AF) has become an essential instrument for achieving the objective of capacity building and safeguarding vulnerable nations from the damaging effects of climate change. While global dialogue has focused on mitigation strategies, growing recognition of the irreversibility of certain climate impacts has intensified attention on how societies can be financially equipped to adapt to a changing climate. In this context, the AF domain is experiencing increased interest from both practitioners and academics; however, there is a lack of comprehensive studies mapping this area of knowledge. The present research addresses this gap by utilizing three methodological approaches to map the intellectual and social framework of the AF field. A scientometric analysis was conducted using CiteSpace software to create networks of authors, countries, keywords, and institutions involved in AF publications, highlighting the predominance of contributions from developed nations, with limited research participation from developing countries. Second, cluster analysis was performed using Python, employing TF‐IDF matrix and K‐means clustering yielding seven distinct clusters: Climate Adaptation Funding and Policy, Private Sector Engagement, Economic Impacts, Global Initiatives and Policies, Adaptation Coordination and Implementation, Risk Management, and Local Community‐Based Initiatives. Third, content analysis of 62 recent studies, combined with scientometric and clustering techniques, was conducted to identify promising future research directions. Implications for various stakeholders are discussed.</jats:p>

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This article summarizes the evolution of portfolio theory from mean–variance optimization to AI‐augmented investment systems. Rather than treating portfolio models as isolated techniques, it organizes the literature as a sequence of responses to different forms of uncertainty: variance, systematic risk, expected‐return estimation error, downside risk, tail loss, parameter ambiguity, risk‐budgeting instability, conditional volatility, regime dependence, high‐dimensional prediction, and AI governance. Combining a systematic literature review, public‐metadata bibliometric analysis, and thematic synthesis, the article covers leading academic journals and practitioner‐oriented outlets, including JF, JFE, RFS, RF, JFQA, Management Science, FAJ, JPM, FMPM, and JAM. The survey highlights how classical portfolio theory, CAPM and multifactor allocation, Bayesian/Black–Litterman models, CVaR, robust optimization, risk parity, volatility management, regime‐switching allocation, parametric portfolio policies, machine learning, and LLM‐based agents form a cumulative intellectual architecture.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>The article is designed as a compact roadmap for doctoral students, academic researchers, and quantitative researchers in hedge funds and asset management who seek a rapid but rigorous understanding of how portfolio theory has evolved and how its core problems remain relevant in the AI era.</jats:p>

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Green bonds are important financial instruments in sustainable finance, generating a rapidly expanding academic literature. This paper identifies the topics analyzed in green bond academic research and examines how these topics are associated with journal and post‐publication diffusion metrics. Using 1048 paper abstracts published between 2015 and 2024, Latent Dirichlet Allocation identifies five topics: sustainable development finance, greenium, carbon emissions, market connectedness and issuer performance. Papers investigating the greenium, carbon emissions, market connectedness and issuer performance are associated with publication in higher impact factor journals and higher average academic citations. The greenium topic is also associated with higher policy and news citations, suggesting broader post‐publication diffusion beyond academia. In contrast, papers with an emphasis on sustainable development finance are associated with lower journal impact factors and lower post‐publication diffusion. The findings provide insights for researchers, policymakers and journal editors into how different topics of green bond research circulate across scholarly, policy and media domains.</jats:p>

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This paper surveys infrastructure project finance and investment management through the organizing concept of bankability. It explains how long‐lived, capital‐intensive and politically exposed infrastructure assets are transformed into financeable projects and investable claims through special‐purpose vehicles, contractual risk allocation, cash‐flow controls, public support, credit structuring and capital recycling. The survey connects project‐finance practice with economic questions in incomplete contracting, public‐private risk sharing, financial intermediation, institutional investment, energy transition and ESG risk management. It argues that infrastructure finance is best understood not as a simple public‐versus‐private funding choice, but as a system for allocating construction, revenue, political, operating, currency, refinancing and ESG risks to parties able to manage, absorb or price them. The paper concludes with a research and practitioner agenda on bankability measurement, debt capacity, secondary markets, blended finance, and climate‐resilient infrastructure investment.</jats:p>

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Narrative disclosure has become an essential component of corporate communication as digital technologies reshape how firms interact with stakeholders. The rise of e‐government and corporate digital transformation has been accompanied by profound changes in corporate disclosure practices, including greater transparency, wider adoption of digital reporting, and the expansion of disclosure across ESG reports, corporate websites, and FinTech platforms. This study systematically reviews 205 articles published between 2010 and early 2026 using the Theory, Context, Characteristics, and Methodology (TCCM) framework. The review finds that prior research primarily examines linguistic characteristics, including tone, readability, complexity, sentiment, uncertainty, and forward‐looking language. These characteristics function as outcomes of firm, governance, managerial, and institutional factors while influencing the judgments and decisions of investors, analysts, auditors, creditors, consumers, and digital platform users. The review also reveals a shift from traditional disclosure settings to digital communication environments. Methodologically, the literature is dominated by archival data, econometric analysis, and computational text analysis, whereas qualitative, experimental, and mixed method studies remain less common. By synthesizing fragmented evidence, this study develops an integrated understanding of how e‐government and corporate digital transformation jointly reshape corporate narrative disclosure. It also identifies theoretical, methodological, and contextual gaps to guide future research.</jats:p>

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The valuation of renewable energy investments conventionally assumes that electricity prices are exogenous, an assumption that fails once wind and solar reach a substantial share of the electricity supply. Because wind and solar generation is highly correlated across producers, large‐scale deployment depresses wholesale electricity prices during periods of high renewable output, reducing project revenues, a phenomenon known as revenue cannibalization. This review synthesizes the literature on renewable energy investment in the presence of revenue cannibalization, spanning investment appraisal methodologies, the diagnosis of cannibalization, and the modeling of mitigation strategies. Our analysis reveals that many valuation methods frequently neglect this endogenous price risk, and that existing research lacks an integrated framework for evaluating mitigation strategies, such as storage and sector coupling, from an investor's perspective. We propose a two‐level framework to bridge this gap between project‐level valuation and systemic market risk.</jats:p>

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) has become an important multidimensional research method and is now widely used in business and economics. This study adopts a scoping‐review approach and uses Natural Language Processing (NLP), a data‐driven machine‐learning technique, to analyze 12,686 relevant studies and classify the literature into major research themes and categories. Specifically, we identify three DEA‐related themes, CoreDEA (11,167 studies), StatDEA (1266 studies), and DecisionDEA (253 studies), which can be further divided into 15 categories, including Dynamic DEA, Undesirable DEA, Bootstrap DEA, and ANP/AHP DEA. The findings show that traditional DEA methods, especially those within CoreDEA, continue to develop actively. At the same time, the growing prominence of sustainability‐related research suggests that SBM DEA and hybrid models incorporating bootstrap, meta‐frontier, and network DEA may represent an important direction for future research.</jats:p>

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Against the backdrop of digital economy development and global economic momentum transformation, the integration of artificial intelligence and InsurTech has become a key driver of high‐quality economic growth. Based on 137 empirical papers from the Web of Science Core Collection (2012–2026), this paper conducts a bibliometric analysis to systematically review the research evolution, core themes, methodologies and global distribution of AI–InsurTech integration, focusing on its economic effects and momentum transmission mechanisms. Results show that studies have shifted from technology application to economic efficiency and institutional governance, forming five core knowledge clusters. Micro‐level research dominates while macroeconomic analysis remains insufficient. The global research pattern features the rapid rise of Asia and steady development in Europe and the US, and empirical methods are moving toward rigorous causal identification. We identify three major gaps in theoretical mechanisms, causal identification and institutional ethics, and propose future research directions. This study clarifies the logic of technology–finance integration driving economic momentum transformation and provides implications for theory and policy.</jats:p>

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Rapid urbanization and large‐scale rural‐to‐urban labor migration in China have reshaped the development landscape of urban‐rural basic education. This paper aims to systematically synthesize and review the literature on the impact of labor migration on urban‐rural basic education integration. The review first analyzes the impact mechanisms of migration on the supply and demand of education, the efficiency and equity of resource allocation in urban and rural areas from multiple disciplinary perspectives. Subsequently, it clarifies that labor migration, by disrupting the supply and demand of education, causing spatial misallocation of resources, and creating friction with the static household registration system, exerts multi‐dimensional and complex inhibitory effects on the integration of urban and rural education. Finally, it reveals that the ultimate impact shows significant non‐linear, conditional, and heterogeneous features, conditional on key moderators such as institutional responses, family capital, and regional conditions. The realization of future integration lies in building an education finance and planning mechanism that can dynamically respond to population distribution, empowering quality integration through digital technology, promoting the characteristic development of rural small‐scale schools, and dismantling institutional barriers such as household registration and school progression constraints, thereby promoting the high‐quality and systematic integration of urban‐rural basic education.</jats:p>

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    This study uses a hybrid methodology of bibliometric analysis and systematic review to critically review the existing research on corporate digital transformation (CDT) effects published between 2018 and 2025. Descriptive analysis shows that this research field was still in its infancy before 2022 and experienced an explosive growth period thereafter. China takes the lead in publication volume, while
                    <jats:italic>Finance Research Letters</jats:italic>
                    emerges as the most prolific journal and research results are predominantly concentrated in domains such as finance and economics. Keyword and thematic analysis indicate that “digital transformation” is the core keyword, and research themes have gradually expanded from basic dimensions like firm performance to diverse areas including ESG, supply chain management, and risk management. The evolution of CDT effects research proceeds along the lines of technological determinism, organizational adaptation, and social construction. This study advances a systematic understanding of the CDT effects by developing a bibliometric overview of relevant research and illustrating the field's conceptual framework and thematic interconnections. The findings offer empirical insights to guide managers in formulating differentiated digital strategies and assist policymakers in constructing supportive ecosystems for digital transformation.
                  </jats:p>

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The livelihood resilience of smallholder farmers has become an important issue affecting food security and rural development. This paper presents a systematic review of 135 important publications on smallholders’ livelihood resilience from 2009 to 2025, covering the framework and methods of measurement, influencing factors, and strategies and practices. We find that the authors studying smallholders’ livelihood resilience mainly come from China, and the research topics are strongly related to macro policies. Second, the major frameworks of measurement include sustainable livelihoods framework, socio‐ecological system resilience framework, household livelihood resilience approach, vulnerability framework and resilience index measurement and analysis framework. The research methods include quantitative, qualitative, and mixed approaches. Third, the livelihood resilience of smallholder farmers is influenced by multidimensional factors, such as livelihood capital, household geographic characteristics, market and value chain, climate change. Fourth, there are many strategies and practices for enhancing livelihood resilience of smallholder farmers, including agroecological and technological system innovation, livelihood diversification and capacity building, institutional strengthening and empowerment, knowledge systems and innovation support. Finally, the existing research is marked by inconsistent measurement frameworks, insufficient longitudinal data, and limited policy universality. Future research should identify resilience thresholds, target vulnerable groups, and develop actionable monitoring tools for policymakers.</jats:p>

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>We perform a complex quantitative synthesis of the effects of macroeconomic news announcements on exchange rates based on 985 estimates from 31 primary studies. We advance testing for publication selection by combining standard visual inspection of funnel plot and employment of the FAT‐PET‐MRA asymmetry tests with the use of modern alternative testing techniques. Our analysis finds evidence consistent with publication selection, which persists after including the moderator variables. Once it is accounted for, the mean effect beyond bias is close to zero. The sources of heterogeneity in the estimates are primarily driven by methodological and technical differences across studies, in particular the length of the event window and the construction of the surprise measure. Next part of the variation in the reported effects is associated with the country of the news announcement, the interest rate environment and the affiliation of the authors.</jats:p>

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This survey reviews the macroeconomic literature on market power, focusing on its measurement, determinants, and macroeconomic effects. It synthesizes evidence from concentration ratios, business dynamism indicators, and markup/markdown estimates, documenting a distinct change in trends since the 1980s, especially in the United States. Aggregate patterns are characterized by stable median markups alongside rising upper‐tail dispersion and reallocation toward a small set of high‐markup firms, while developments across Europe and other economies are more heterogeneous and context‐dependent. A central theme is the unresolved tension between technology‐based explanations—emphasizing scale economies, automation, and intangibles—and competition‐based explanations stressing conduct, entry barriers, and regulation. The evidence linking market power to declining labor shares, rising profits, and increasing wage dispersion and inequality is strong, while effects on productivity, investment, and innovation are more nuanced and non‐monotonic. The survey provides a methodological assessment, reconciles competing interpretations, and discusses implications for macroeconomic and competition policy.</jats:p>

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Driven by the rapid expansion of the digital economy and changing sociopsychological needs, emotion‐driven consumption has evolved from an individual psychological behavior into a phenomenon affecting consumer welfare and household finance. This paper provides a systematic review of 197 high‐quality studies on emotions and consumer behavior published between 2000 and May 2026. The main findings are as follows. First, the number of relevant publications has increased steadily, while also exhibiting pronounced trends toward international collaboration and interdisciplinary integration. Second, existing studies primarily rely on micro‐level individual data, while econometric models remain the dominant empirical method. Third, the formation of emotion‐driven consumption is jointly shaped by psychological and behavioral characteristics, individual and household attributes, and external environmental stimuli. Fourth, under moderate and rational constraints, emotion‐driven consumption can promote consumption upgrading; however, in the absence of such constraints, it may impair physical and mental health, exacerbate household financial vulnerability, and increase short‐term market volatility and consumer credit risk. Fifth, the existing literature still faces several limitations, and future research should strengthen interdisciplinary theoretical integration, construct long‐term multidimensional databases, and combine natural experiments with machine learning methods.</jats:p>

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Rural labor migration has profoundly reshaped the rural social structures and agrifood systems, whereby left‐behind elderly groups have become pivotal actors for rural inclusive development. Traditional rural development research generally adopts a macroeconomic or institutional perspective, overlooking the micro endogenous mechanism of individual elderly wellbeing that underpins rural inclusive development. Based on Amartya Sen's capability approach, this theory‐driven systematic literature review constructs a micro‐to‐macro analytical framework to clarify the transmission mechanism linking elderly wellbeing differentiation, feasible capability stratification and inclusive development. It also highlights the empowerment effect of digitalization on elderly capability improvement and alleviation of opportunity deprivation. Different from conventional macro‐oriented rural development studies, this research reshapes the theoretical cognition of rural elderly as value creators rather than passive vulnerable recipients. This review confirms that rural inclusive development cannot be achieved solely through top‐down institutional improvement or resource input. The substantive realization of rural inclusiveness essentially relies on the equalization of individual feasible capabilities and the full release of the left‐behind elderly vulnerable groups’ substantive freedom. This review highlights the theoretical value of focusing on left‐behind elderly groups in rural development research, providing a systematic theoretical reference and literature synthesis for future micro‐level empirical exploration and targeted inclusive rural progress.</jats:p>

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Millions of smallholder farmers in Asia and Sub‐Saharan Africa have been crowded out of institutional lending. While unclear property rights or illiquid collateral, isolation, the lack of tailored credit products, and agricultural endowment risks hinder their access to credit from formal channels, the extant literature is scant in mapping barriers and enablers to institutional lending for smallholders and presenting them in a unified framework by integrating theoretical perspectives into a conceptual synthesis. We bridge this gap by conducting an integrative review that combines a bibliometric analysis of 848 articles retrieved from the Scopus database, a systematic literature review of 83 articles, and 29 grey literature sources, utilizing an integrated Antecedents‐Decisions‐Outcomes (ADO) and Theory‐Context‐Characteristic‐Method (TCCM) framework. We identify supply‐side and demand‐side antecedents (barriers) that inform farmer borrowing decisions, lenders’ screening and credit appraisal, and the choice of intermediation channel, thereby shaping farmer credit availability and access, farm investment and agricultural yields, and social and environmental outcomes. The theoretical perspectives emerging from the TCCM framework are categorized into the structural, behavioural, and network layers that affect transaction‐cost attributes of institutional lending. We propose future research directions to address the conceptual and empirical gaps to deepen institutional lending to small‐scale farmers.</jats:p>

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>We address an important research gap by quantifying the association between weather conditions (sunshine, rainfall, temperature anomalies) and individual financial, mental and physical health self‐assessments. We compile a unique dataset of  observations (1991–2018) by matching individual‐level data (covering 380 Local Authorities) from the British Household Panel & UK Household Longitudinal Surveys to monthly and daily data from 32 weather stations. We provide robust evidence that favourable climatic conditions are positively related to the likelihood of reporting higher well‐being assessments, and negatively related to adverse conditions (particularly temperature anomalies). The estimated weather monetary cost reaches 15% of monthly household income.</jats:p>

                  <jats:p>This study examines the relationship between religiosity and vaccine hesitancy. I reveal a robust negative and non‐linear association between church attendance and COVID‐19 vaccination rates across Polish municipalities. Utilising survey data, I find that more religious individuals are less likely to accept the COVID19 vaccine, and their willingness decreases with higher local‐level religiosity, suggesting the presence of peer effects. I also examine how believers' lower vaccine acceptance is shaped by both direct and mediated effects in the mediation analysis.</jats:p>

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Cointegrating rank selection is studied in a function space reduced rank regression where the data are time series of cross‐section curves. Consistent cointegrating rank estimation is developed using information criteria extended to curve time series environments. The asymptotic theory involves two‐parameter Gaussian processes that generalise the standard limit processes involved in cointegrating regressions. Simulations provide evidence of the effectiveness of consistent rank selection by the BIC criterion and the tendency of AIC to overestimate order as in standard lag order selection in autoregression, as well as in reduced rank regression with multiple time series.</jats:p>

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>A central assumption for identifying structural shocks in vector autoregressive (VAR) models via heteroskedasticity is the time‐invariance of the impact effects of the shocks. It is shown how that assumption can be tested when long‐run restrictions based on the cointegration structure of the variables are available for identifying structural shocks. The importance of performing such tests is illustrated by investigating the impact of fundamental shocks on stock prices in the U.S. It is found that fundamental shocks post‐1986 have become more important than in the pre‐1986 period.</jats:p>

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Accurate poverty measurement relies on household consumption data, but such data are often inadequate, outdated, or display inconsistencies over time in poorer countries. To address these data challenges, we employ survey‐to‐survey imputation to produce estimates for several poverty indicators including headcount poverty, extreme poverty, poverty gap, near‐poverty rates, as well as mean consumption levels and the entire consumption distribution. Analysing 22 multi‐topic household surveys conducted over the past decade in Bangladesh, Ethiopia, Malawi, Nigeria, Tanzania, and Vietnam, we find encouraging results. Adding either household utility expenditures or food expenditures to basic imputation models with household‐level demographic, employment, and asset variables could improve the probability of imputation accuracy between 0.1 and 0.4. Adding predictors from geospatial data could further increase imputation accuracy. The analysis also shows that a larger time interval between surveys is associated with a lower probability of predicting some poverty indicators, and that a better imputation model goodness‐of‐fit (
                    <jats:italic>R</jats:italic>
                    <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                    ) does not necessarily help. The results offer cost‐saving inputs into future survey design.

10.1111/obes.70109.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The 2016 EU referendum result was widely perceived as a statement against immigration. This paper investigates whether information about majority voting outcomes influences attitudes towards immigrants. Using a survey experiment conducted in England in 2017–2018, we randomly exposed participants to truthful information indicating that local constituencies had predominantly voted either to Leave or to Remain in the 2016 EU referendum. The intervention substantially shifted beliefs about local Brexit vote shares. Although we find no statistically significant effects on most individual survey questions, exposure to a Leave‐majority signal leads to more restrictive immigration policy preferences relative to exposure to a Remain‐majority signal. Effects are concentrated among participants for whom the information was politically dissonant or unexpected. Overall, the pattern of results is consistent with a conformity mechanism operating through perceived majority views, suggesting that referenda may continue to shape expressed policy preferences beyond their immediate aftermath.</jats:p>

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Leveraging over 40 million residential electricity billing records from more than one million meters in Ethiopia, we test whether consumers respond to marginal prices at kink points under an increasing block tariff (IBT). We exploit a unique institutional setting in which two distinct billing systems (manual postpaid and automated prepaid) operate under a common IBT within a state‐owned utility, allowing us to test whether observed bunching reflects behavioural responses or measurement error. In the raw postpaid data, we observe bunching at kink points, but this bunching disappears after normalizing for billing‐cycle length and aggregating readings to smooth billing anomalies, suggesting the spikes reflect the billing process rather than underlying behavioural responses to marginal prices. In contrast, prepaid data show no bunching at kink points but exhibit spikes at round‐number recharge amounts, suggesting rule‐of‐thumb purchasing behaviour. These findings highlight that, in a setting with low electricity prices, no evidence of marginal price responses, and widespread shared connections, the IBT is unlikely to achieve its intended goals of subsidy targeting, conservation, and cost recovery.</jats:p>

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    We examine the impact of an integrated parenting program designed to improve parent–child interactions. Exploiting experimental variation in program access, we show that the intervention improves the overall parenting practice index by 0.38 standard deviations and increases parental material investments by 0.64 standard deviations. We also find improvements in children's health, including a 3‐percentage‐point reduction in the prevalence of wasting and a rightward shift in the distribution of weight‐for‐height
                    <jats:italic>z</jats:italic>
                    ‐scores. These results suggest that augmenting standard nutritional counselling with a parenting curriculum focused on stimulation and child protection can generate meaningful gains in children's long‐term well‐being.
                  </jats:p>

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This paper studies inequality of opportunity (IOp) in individual net wealth in Germany from 2002 to 2019 using the Socio‐Economic Panel (SOEP). Applying the ex‐ante IOp framework, we quantify the share of wealth inequality attributable to immutable circumstances and benchmark it against IOp in gross labour earnings. Relative IOp in net wealth is high—slightly above one half of total wealth inequality—and stable over time, whereas relative IOp in labour earnings declines and converges towards the wealth level by the end of the study period. Decomposing net wealth into financial, real estate and business components shows similar and stable IOp levels for financial and housing wealth, but substantially higher and more variable IOp for business wealth. Across all components, childhood and parental circumstances are the dominant drivers of wealth IOp, while place effects matter most for real estate wealth and gender for business wealth. In contrast, gender and demographics are the main contributors to IOp in labour earnings.</jats:p>

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    This paper develops panel variance ratio statistics to examine serial dependence in time series with cross‐sectional dependence. We derive asymptotic properties for panels where the cross‐section dimension  is fixed or grows with
                    <jats:italic>T</jats:italic>
                    . Using a factor structure to explain cross‐sectional dependence, we propose a common correlation effects approach to eliminate latent factor influence. By leveraging an increasing
                    <jats:italic>N</jats:italic>
                    , our new pooled defactorized variance ratio statistic remains consistent over long horizons even when  grows at the same rate as
                    <jats:italic>T</jats:italic>
                    , unlike univariate statistics. We compare its performance to a standardized pooled variance ratio across alternatives with distinct long‐run dependence patterns for both large and finite samples. Applying our tests to size and industry stock return portfolios, we find strong predictability in both short‐ and long‐term horizons, with the common factor primarily shaping serial dependence patterns.
                  </jats:p>

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>In VECMs (or CVARs), the weak exogeneity of some of the variables (for the long‐run parameters) is related to the equilibrium adjustment dynamics. This has sometimes led to the statistical concept of weak exogeneity being given a causal interpretation. This paper analyses the causal informational value of weak exogeneity, using graphical representations of causal structures, to show when such an interpretation is valid. We specifically consider the identification of the driving variables, and their relationship to non‐causality. We demonstrate that causal interpretations of weak exogeneity may not hold when relevant variables are omitted. Our exploration of the conditions under which weak exogeneity conveys causal information helps further the study of long‐run causal inference.</jats:p>

10.1111/obes.70115.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    We analyse growth vulnerability in the four largest Euro Area (EA) economies, measured as a lower quantile of the growth distribution conditional on EA‐wide and country‐specific macroeconomic/financial factors. Growth densities are obtained under a
                    <jats:italic>normal</jats:italic>
                    activity scenario and under
                    <jats:italic>stressed</jats:italic>
                    conditions. We find that vulnerability is higher in Germany, more exposed to EA‐wide conditions, and in Spain, with large country‐specific dynamics. Under stress, financial factors amplify adverse macroeconomic conditions, and even severe individual shocks fail to fully explain the vulnerability observed under systemic stress. Our results underscore the importance of monitoring local and EA‐wide macro‐financial conditions to mitigate vulnerability.
                  </jats:p>

10.1111/obes.70116.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This paper examines how alternative surcharge designs affect market outcomes in the New York City (NYC) Yellow Cab system. We study two distinct policies: a congestion surcharge that raises passenger fares without directly compensating drivers, and a rush‐hour surcharge that provides time‐based incentives to drivers during periods of high demand. Using a regression discontinuity in time framework, we exploit discrete changes in fares to identify the causal effects of these surcharges on trip volume. We find that the congestion surcharge reduces demand for short‐distance trips but does not generate measurable improvements in traffic conditions, suggesting a shift in trip composition rather than effective congestion mitigation. In contrast, the rush‐hour surcharge leads to an immediate increase in trip volume at the policy threshold, consistent with a supply‐side response to driver incentives. Although both policies increase fares, they operate through distinct economic mechanisms and are identified from different sources of variation. Our findings highlight that the effects of fare increases depend critically on policy design‐specifically, whether pricing operates as a tax on passengers or as an incentive for drivers. More broadly, the results underscore the importance of distinguishing between demand‐ and supply‐side channels when evaluating pricing interventions in regulated transportation markets.</jats:p>

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Test scores provide objective indicators of student achievement, but are argued to neglect certain skills. Teacher assessments, conversely, are subjective but typically designed to provide a more holistic evaluation of student potential. Combining survey and administrative data for the Netherlands, we estimate the predictive power of test scores and teacher assessments measured at age 12 across the life cycle, and analyse what this predictive power reflects. We find that the non‐overlapping predictive power of both indicators is strong. While the predictive power of the teacher assessment is partially driven by socio‐economic bias, self‐fulfilling prophecy effects and, especially, test measurement error, we find that it also captures productive skills that tests do not.</jats:p>

10.1111/obes.70118.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    We study how both
                    <jats:italic>who</jats:italic>
                    we talk about when we talk about inequality and
                    <jats:italic>how</jats:italic>
                    we talk about it shape redistributive preferences. In a nationally representative survey experiment in Germany with a 1‐year follow‐up, we exogenously vary the focus of attention (top 10% vs. bottom 10%) and the mode of delivery (subtle priming vs. factual information about the share of total income earned by that group). We examine effects on perceived inequality, general support for redistribution and concrete tax‐based policy preferences. We find three main results. First, simply directing attention to different ends of the distribution shifts support for redistribution. Second, corrective information about the richest 10% generates larger belief updates and stronger short‐run changes in attitudes than information about the poorest 10%. Third, these effects fade within a year, underscoring the limited durability of one‐off interventions. These findings help reconcile mixed evidence from prior inequality‐information experiments by highlighting the importance of both the
                    <jats:italic>focus</jats:italic>
                    and the
                    <jats:italic>mode</jats:italic>
                    of communication in shaping effect size and persistence. We discuss implications for the design of redistribution policy communication and for measuring belief dynamics.
                  </jats:p>

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>We examine the relationship between the assignment of homework and student achievement among 8th grade students across 23 countries using the TIMSS 2019 dataset. Exploiting within‐student, between‐subject variation in homework assignment, we find a small but statistically significant positive relationship between homework and achievement. This benefit is driven primarily by the frequency with which homework is assigned rather than its volume. Heterogeneity analyses suggest larger benefits for students with more highly qualified or more experienced teachers, while effects are broadly uniform across the performance distribution except among particularly weak students. We also document substantial cross‐country variability in these estimated effects.</jats:p>

10.1111/obes.70120.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>We propose a new model of revenue‐maximising lottery pricing under income‐related heterogeneity and apply it to 13 years of UK National Lottery data. Our pricing rule shows how a state's lottery power is shaped by heterogeneities in lotto demand and the income distribution, and we study its efficiency and distributional implications. We find that UK lotto was regressive, underpriced by up to 20% for Saturday games and overpriced by up to 20% for Wednesday games. But annual revenue losses reached only 3% (£57m) and legislated pricing was less regressive than optimal on Saturdays and more regressive on Wednesdays. We contrast results from our model with those of two extensions: 1. a dynamic, rollover‐induced, model of revenue‐maximising pricing and 2. a model of social welfare maximisation with a lotto revenue target.</jats:p>

10.1111/obes.70121.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Temperature can play an important role in time allocation decisions like labour supply as workers seek to avoid harmful exposure or enjoy higher utility from leisure. Using time use survey data, we estimate the effect of temperature on labour supply in the UK. We find large reductions in working time on high‐temperature days, especially among weather‐exposed workers. While the time use patterns we document are consistent with avoidance behaviours, we cannot rule out leisure as an alternative mechanism. We also show that low‐income workers are constrained in their ability to adjust their labour supply in response to high temperatures.</jats:p>

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>We estimate the impact of Eximbank Hungary's working capital loans on firm exports using matching and panel methods. Loans increase export value by about 20% and export share by 6.5%. The strongest point estimates are associated with first loans. Export gains persist over time, but robust long‐run effects are detectable only at the full‐sample level, not among firms that receive a single loan. The estimated coefficients decline by initial export share but do not vary by firm size and productivity. Loans raise sales and employment by about 10% but do not affect productivity and profitability.</jats:p>

10.1111/obes.70126.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The strict confinement implemented by the National Government of Colombia in 2020 to contain the expansion of the COVID‐19 pandemic created challenges in data collection operations conducted through household surveys. As a result, surveys that traditionally relied on face‐to‐face collection methods transitioned to a remote mode using telephone surveys. We exploit a quasi‐experimental design based on the geographical‐temporal exogenous variation in the collection mode of the leading household survey for the Colombian labour market and the linkage of this survey to the nationwide social security administrative record to measure the impact of the change in the collection mode on the reported salaried labour income. We find that the change in collection mode reduces the measured salaried labour income by approximately 4.4 percentage points and increases its variance and dispersion, with differences between population groups. These findings have implications for the development of mixed data collection methods and the analysis of income‐based statistics.</jats:p>
